questions.q: What does a single neuron compute?
options: A weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation function
The average of its inputs with no weights
A decision tree split on one feature
A distance to the nearest training example
questions.explain: A neuron is a linear regression (weighted sum plus bias) followed by an activation function.

questions.q: Which familiar model is equivalent to a neural network with a single neuron and a sigmoid activation?
options: K-means clustering
Random forest
Logistic regression
Naive Bayes
questions.explain: Logistic regression is a weighted sum passed through a sigmoid: a one-neuron network.

questions.q: In the ring-shaped example, why did logistic regression score only about 0.54?
options: It had too many features
It can only draw one straight boundary, and the classes are not linearly separable
It was trained on the test set
Logistic regression cannot be used for two classes
questions.explain: One neuron gives one straight decision boundary, which cannot separate one group sitting inside another.

questions.q: What do hidden layers give a network that a single neuron lacks?
options: The ability to learn non-linear patterns and its own intermediate features
Guaranteed 100 percent accuracy
Freedom from needing any training data
Automatic removal of outliers
questions.explain: Each hidden neuron is a small regression whose output becomes a feature for the next layer, allowing curved boundaries.

questions.q: In the numpy example, the weights [0.5, -2.0] and bias 1.0 were used. Where do weights come from in a real model?
options: A person chooses them by hand
They are learned from training data
They are always set to zero
They come from the test set
questions.explain: The example weights were invented for illustration; real weights are learned from data during training (lesson 3).
